name: Drug Repurposing
title: Drug Repurposing
answer: Drug repurposing is the search for new uses for medicines that are already approved or well studied, rather than designing a molecule from scratch. In an AI context it covers the models that scan molecular structures, gene expression, clinical records and published literature to propose a compound for a disease it was not originally intended to treat. It sits inside drug discovery and molecular simulation because much of the work is done computationally before any wet lab experiment. The field overlaps with knowledge graphs, protein structure prediction and real world evidence analysis.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drug repurposing is the search for new uses for medicines that are already approved or well studied, rather than designing a molecule from scratch. In an AI context it covers the models that scan molecular structures, gene expression, clinical records and published literature to propose a compound for a disease it was not originally intended to treat. It sits inside drug discovery and molecular simulation because much of the work is done computationally before any wet lab experiment. The field overlaps with knowledge graphs, protein structure prediction and real world evidence analysis.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large compound and target databases, electronic health records, biobank data and text corpora such as PubMed. Models range from graph neural networks over molecular graphs to transformer models over biomedical text, and increasingly to protein structure predictors used to check whether a drug can bind a new target. Training and inference need GPU clusters, and the data pipelines need careful record linkage between chemistry, biology and patient data. Many groups run these pipelines on cloud infrastructure because the storage and compute demands are bursty.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical study starts by building a representation of drugs and diseases, then scoring every drug disease pair for plausibility. Common approaches include signature matching, where a drug's transcriptional effect is compared against a disease signature, network proximity, where drug targets and disease genes are measured for closeness in a protein interaction network, and knowledge graph embedding, where links between drugs, genes and phenotypes are learned. Predictions are filtered for toxicity, dosing and prior trial failures, then tested in cell lines, organoids or animal models before any human study. Validation is the slow part, and a computational hit is only a hypothesis until it survives an experiment.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Repurposing leans on drugs with known safety profiles, but a new indication still needs its own evidence on dose, interactions and the population that will take it. Off label prescribing, compassionate use and trial enrolment each carry different consent and reporting duties, and patient data used to generate hypotheses falls under privacy rules such as HIPAA and GDPR. Provenance matters because a repurposing claim may rest on a model whose training data, version and assumptions are not documented.This is a description of practice, not legal or medical advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near term direction is tighter coupling between prediction and experiment, with automated labs testing ranked candidates and feeding results back into the models. Foundation models trained across chemistry, proteins and clinical text are being adapted to repurposing tasks, and regulators are being asked to review evidence generated partly by models. The main open problems are causal inference from observational data, batch effects and bias in biobanks, and the fact that most repurposing candidates still fail in phase two trials. Progress will depend as much on data quality and trial design as on model size.
